lesson.title: The -é Past
lesson.subtitle: The passé composé with avoir: j'ai mangé, tu as parlé — where -é is English -ed

hook.title: One Tense for Both 'I Ate' and 'I Have Eaten'
hook.content: English agonizes over the difference between 'I ate' and 'I have eaten'. Spoken French sweeps that distinction off the table: one single two-word past tense — le passé composé — covers BOTH! You already own the first piece: the present tense of avoir (j'ai, tu as, il a, nous avons, vous avez). For the second piece, every -er verb simply swaps -er for -é (pronounced /e/, the exact same sound as the infinitive!): parler → parlé ('spoken'), manger → mangé ('eaten'), décider → décidé ('decided').

footnotes.title: Why -é and -er sound 100% identical
footnotes.content: Both -er (/e/) and -é (/e/) lost their final Latin consonants (parlāre → parler, parlātum → parlé). Your ear tells them apart purely by what sits in front of them: je veux parler (after a verb) vs j'ai parlé (after avoir)!

pattern.title: avoir + Participle (-é, -i, -u)
pattern.content: Three quick rules give you the participles: (1) Every -er verb turns into -é (mangé, parlé, trouvé, donné, aimé, confirmé, réservé). (2) Regular -ir verbs drop the r to end in -i (finir → fini, choisir → choisi). (3) Common irregulars end in -u or -is/-it: voir → vu (as in déjà vu 'already seen'!), prendre/comprendre → pris/compris, faire → fait. And where do ne...pas and déjà go? Right around the auxiliary avoir: Je n'ai pas compris. J'ai déjà mangé!
pattern.linguist_note: Latin habēre + perfect passive participle grammaticalized across Western Romance into the primary conversational past.
pattern.trap_note: The shortcut your mind will offer: dropping avoir and saying *Je mangé to translate English 'I ate'. Spoken French ALWAYS builds the past with two words: J'ai mangé!

exercises.prompt: Match each past participle with its English meaning and pattern:
exercises.target_answer: eaten / ate, finished, seen / saw, understood, done / made
exercises.meaning: mangé (-er → -é), fini (-ir → -i), vu (as in déjà vu), compris (prendre family), fait (Latin factum)
exercises.explanation: Every -er verb takes -é; -ir takes -i; voir gives vu; comprendre gives compris; faire gives fait.

exercises.prompt: Build 'I spoke / I have spoken' using avoir + the -é participle of parler:
exercises.meaning: J'ai parlé (I spoke / I have spoken)
exercises.explanation: J'ai + parlé covers both 'I spoke' and 'I have spoken'.

exercises.prompt: What is the word-for-word structure of 'J'ai déjà vu ce film'?
options: I have already seen this film
exercises.target_answer: I have already seen this film
exercises.meaning: Literal structure: I have already seen this film
exercises.explanation: Even when English uses simple past 'I already saw', French uses 'I have already seen' (J'ai déjà vu).

cues: Yesterday, I have eaten the cake → Hier, j'ai mangé le gâteau
exercises.explanation: Hier, j'ai mangé le gâteau uses two words (j'ai mangé) for English 'I ate'.

diagnosis.slip: omitted j'ai or used infinitive manger
diagnosis.cue: Always pair j'ai with the -é participle: j'ai mangé.

exercises.prompt: Listen and write the whole sentence.
exercises.explanation: Tu as compris translates both 'Did you understand?' and 'Have you understood?'.
exercises.affirmation: You heard Tu as compris and la question cleanly.

summary.outcome: Form the passé composé with avoir + participle (-é, -i, vu, compris, fait) to narrate completed past actions.

use_example.german: Hier, j'ai parlé avec mon ami et j'ai compris.
use_example.english: Yesterday, I spoke with my friend and I understood.

summary.takeaway: One two-word tense (avoir + participle) does the job of both 'I did' and 'I have done'.
summary.curiosity_teaser: Up next on Le Pont ([1701] Participle Twins): see how The -é Past leads directly into Participle Twins.

twist.prompt: Ungraded — 'I made a reservation' (use J'ai fait):
twist.explanation: faire → fait ('done/made'): J'ai fait une réservation.

foreshadow.line: Having mastered The -é Past, look ahead to Topic 18 (Motion Takes être), where this machinery expands into the next dimension of French thought.

payoff.text: The foundation from Topic 16 (Days, Months & Dates) now pays off directly inside The -é Past: every sentence here builds on that earlier step.

mangé.etymology_derivation: manger ← Latin manducāre 'to chew'. English 'mange' is the eating disease — the verb came with the Normans' dogs.

décidé.etymology_derivation: dé·cidé — the é IS the -ed. Decided, désigné, marié: the participle twins are everywhere.

parlé.etymology_derivation: parler ← Late Latin parabolāre 'to tell stories' — parable, parley, parliament (the talking-place).

trouvé.etymology_derivation: trover 'to find' — what you found is a trove.

aimé.etymology_derivation: aimer ← ad + estimare 'to estimate'. English 'aim' drifted from the same estimate — aiming is assessing.

fini.etymology_derivation: Latin fīnis 'end, boundary' — finish, final, fine print.

compris.etymology_derivation: prendre → pris, comprendre → compris, apprendre → appris.

pris.etymology_derivation: French uses prendre ('to take') for ordering food and drink, just like English 'I'll take a coffee'.

vu.context_translation: I have already seen this film.
vu.etymology_derivation: English already owns this participle inside 'déjà vu'!

déjà.etymology_derivation: You already know it from déjà vu ('already seen').

e.name: The é/ed Twins
e.phonetic_rule: The past participle in -é /e/ is the English -ed: mangé/manged, décidé/decided, marié/married.
e.historical_linguistics: The Norman conquest put French participles straight into English verb morphology — countless English past tenses ARE French participles wearing English spelling.
e.philological_note: With avoir, the participle never agrees; with être (motion verbs), it does — the one agreement the past asks for.
e.literature_source: Baugh & Cable, A History of the English Language (2002).
